Fixed Width Confidence Interval for a Mean, Distribution Free

Source: R/seq_fwd_dfr_mean.R
seq_fwd_dfr_mean.Rd

Given the data collected so far, checks the stopping rule of the purely sequential fixed width confidence interval for a population mean when the distribution is not specified (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009). The aim is an interval of half width d (full width \(2d\)) around the sample mean with approximately the stated confidence level. The sample size needed depends on the unknown variance, so observations are collected until the sample size reaches the size the current variance estimate calls for.

Usage

seq_fwd_dfr_mean(x, d, conf_level = 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector of the observations collected so far (at least 2).

d

The half width of the confidence interval, in the units of the data: the interval reported is the sample mean plus and minus d, so its full width is \(2d\). A positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level (default 0.95).

na.rm

Logical; should NA values be removed first? Default TRUE. With FALSE, missing values are an error.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and these rows:

lower_limit

The sample mean minus d.

mean

The sample mean, the point estimate.

upper_limit

The sample mean plus d.

optimal_n

The sample size the current data call for, \(\lceil z_{\alpha/2}^2 (S_n^2 + 1/n) / d^2 \rceil\) (NA when the data are constant).

current_n

The number of observations used.

Attributes: is_satisfied (TRUE once current_n is at least optimal_n), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), conf_level, width (the full width \(2d\)), method, variance_unusable (TRUE when the data are constant, so that no variance has been estimated), and notes.

Details

The function does not collect data and keeps no state. Call it after each new observation (or batch), starting once seq_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot observations are in hand, and stop sampling the first time attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

Sampling stops at the first \(n\) (at or beyond the pilot size) with $$n \ge \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{d^2}\left(S_n^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right),$$ where \(S_n^2\) is the sample variance. The \(1/n\) term keeps the rule from being met on a variance estimate that happens to be very small early on; it vanishes as the sample grows. The optimal_n row is the right hand side rounded up, evaluated at the current data. The reported interval is always \(\bar{X}_n \pm d\); it has the stated confidence level, approximately, only once the rule is met. The rule has the form of the stopping rule of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equation 22), with the sample variance as the estimate of the asymptotic variance and their full width \(\omega\) equal to \(2d\).

The confidence level is asymptotic. It rests on the central limit theorem and on the consistency of \(S_n^2\), and is attained in the limit as d shrinks. For wide targets, and for skewed data even at fairly narrow ones, coverage is below the stated level. In simulation (standard deviation 2, nominal 0.95, the pilot of seq_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot() with its defaults, 40,000 replications, Monte Carlo standard error at most 0.002), coverage for normal data was 0.935 at d = 1 (where the required sample size \(n^* = z_{\alpha/2}^2\sigma^2/d^2\) is about 15), 0.942 at d = 0.5 (\(n^*\) about 61), and 0.948 at d = 0.25 (\(n^*\) about 246). For exponential data with the same standard deviation it was 0.960 at d = 1 (where the pilot of 10 is already most of the 15 required) and then far lower: 0.879 at \(n^*\) of 30, and lowest, about 0.855, when \(n^*\) was between 40 and 61 (d = 0.5). It recovered slowly: 0.886 at \(n^*\) of 100, 0.934 at d = 0.25 (\(n^*\) about 246), 0.946 at d = 0.125 (\(n^*\) about 983; 400,000 replications), and still 0.946 at d = 0.0625 (\(n^*\) about 3,934; 10,000 replications, standard error 0.002). Skewness slows the approach to the stated level considerably.

The units of the data. The \(1/n\) term is added to a variance, so it is in the squared units of the data, and the procedure depends on the units in which the data are recorded. It adds up to about \(1/\sigma^2\) observations to the sample size that would otherwise be needed: a negligible number when the standard deviation is 1 or more in the units of the data, and a substantial one when it is much smaller. In simulation with normal data, \(\sigma = 0.25\), and d = 0.1 (\(n^*\) about 24), the average final sample size was 35 and coverage was 0.98. The interval is then conservative, not wrong.

Constant data. If every observation is equal, or equal up to rounding error (a range of no more than \(10^{-10}\) times the largest absolute value, as with gain scores of 0.3 computed as posttest minus pretest), the sample variance is zero, or nothing but rounding error, and under the rule as printed the \(1/n\) term alone would eventually stop the sampling. The function departs from the printed rule deliberately: no variance has been estimated, so the rule is reported as not met, optimal_n is NA, attr(out, "variance_unusable") is TRUE, and a note says so (see smsd_check_methods); data whose real spread is that small beside their size should have a common value subtracted first. The limits are still reported (the sample mean minus and plus d, which involve no variance), but they are then not an interval to report: summary(), glance(), and tidy() return them without the note, so test attr(out, "variance_unusable") before using them.

Extreme units. Data that do vary, but whose spread is so large or so small that the sample variance cannot be represented in double precision (differences among the observations beyond about \(10^{154}\) or below about \(10^{-162}\)), are an error that says to change the units. That case is not reported as a rule not yet met, because collecting more data cannot help.

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot; seq_fwd_norm_mean for the normal theory rule without the \(1/n\) term; ts_fwd_dfr_mean for the two stage procedure; seq_aipe_sm for a mean standardized by its standard deviation.

Other seq_fwd_dfr_mean: seq_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean weekly hours of remote work in a firm, to within half an hour
# with 90% confidence. Hours are right skewed; simulated here.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_fwd_dfr_mean_pilot(d = 0.5, conf_level = 0.90)
hours <- rgamma(m, shape = 4, scale = 2)
out <- seq_fwd_dfr_mean(hours, d = 0.5, conf_level = 0.90)
out
#> Sequential check (fixed width interval (distribution free mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : 112
#>   Target width    : 1
#>   Confidence level: 90%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 6.478901
#>   mean              : 6.978901
#>   upper_limit       : 7.478901
#>   optimal_n         : 112
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# Add one employee at a time until the stopping rule is met.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  hours <- c(hours, rgamma(1, shape = 4, scale = 2))
  out <- seq_fwd_dfr_mean(hours, d = 0.5, conf_level = 0.90)
}
out
#> Sequential check (fixed width interval (distribution free mean))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 150
#>   Criterion n     : 150
#>   Target width    : 1
#>   Confidence level: 90%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 7.177634
#>   mean              : 7.677634
#>   upper_limit       : 8.177634
#>   optimal_n         : 150
#>   current_n         : 150
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
